notes: "One winter night, a swallow came from Africa. 'The monkeys are very sick!' cried Chee-Chee." The swallow arrives but Chee-Chee speaks. It works, but an A1 reader may pause. Optional: "A swallow brought news to Chee-Chee. 'The monkeys are very sick!' he cried."
"Polynesia and Chee-Chee stayed in Africa. People paid to see the Pushmi-pullyu." The scene jumps from Africa to England without a signal. Optional: "Back home, people paid to see the Pushmi-pullyu."
The crocodile is left out entirely at A1. That is fine as condensing.

issues.quote: The doctor gave medicine to the well monkeys, so they stayed well.
issues.problem: 'Well' meaning healthy is used only after a verb ('is well'), not before a noun. 'The well monkeys' sounds wrong to a native speaker, and A2 learners, who know 'well' mainly as an adverb, are likely to misread it.
issues.fix: The doctor gave medicine to the healthy monkeys, so they did not get sick.

notes: "At home, people paid to see the Pushmi-pullyu. Soon the doctor was rich. He went back to Puddleby..." 'At home' followed by 'went back to Puddleby' reads a little oddly. Consider 'Back in England, people paid...'.
"Dab-Dab tied a rope to a tree on land." It is not said how she got there. Optional: 'Dab-Dab flew to land with a rope and tied it to a tree.'
"At home, the doctor took the Pushmi-pullyu to country fairs... and returned to his little house in Puddleby." Same 'at home' / 'returned home' wobble as A2. Consider 'Back in England'.

"He needs money for a new ship for the sailor": B1 never says the first ship was destroyed, only that it 'hit a rock'. Readers will infer it, but adding 'and broke' to the wreck sentence would make it explicit.
"Birds carried his name to other countries" is acceptable but slightly flat; 'Birds carried the news of him to other countries' is more idiomatic.
No conditionals or passives found. Grammar fits B1.

issues.quote: Thousands of swallows came to guide the ship home.
issues.problem: The ship they came on was wrecked, and the text has just said the doctor 'owed the sailor a new ship'. 'The ship' therefore has no referent, and the reader is left wondering what ship they are sailing home in.
issues.fix: Once they had found another ship, thousands of swallows came to guide them home.

notes: 'A parrot who was nearly two hundred years old' is a fair rounding of the original.
'The first man ever to see the Bridge of Apes' sensibly avoids the original's racial wording. Good.

Quiz Q3, "Why was the doctor able to give up showing the Pushmi-pullyu?" The text never says he gave up showing it; it only says he 'returned to his little house a rich man'. This is defensible but indirect. Consider 'How did the doctor become rich again?' with the same keyed answer, and swap the weak distractor 'The sailor returned his ship.'
'Her fears came true' links Sarah's complaint about untidiness to patients leaving, which is a slight stretch. Acceptable.
Prose is genuinely literary (inversion, participle openers, irony with the lion 'merely passing') without padding. The closing exchange follows the original well.

summary: A faithful, child-safe condensation of Lofting's novel. It omits the Jolliginki/Bumpo and pirate episodes, which is acceptable softening and condensing, and it has no film elements. Two levels fail on concrete points: A2 uses the non-idiomatic 'the well monkeys', and B2 refers to 'the ship' going home after the original ship was wrecked and needs replacing. A1, B1 and C1 pass, with only minor notes.
